newsitem.title: FRANCE: German gold woes good news for French Socialists.
newsitem.headline: German gold woes good news for French Socialists.

text.p: Germany's embattled plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves can only be seen as good news for a French Socialist party which hopes to win power in an election runoff next Sunday and is arguing for a more flexibility in the decisions on who will be starters in European monetary union.

The Bonn government said after a stinging rebuke from the Bundesbank on Wednesday it planned to proceed with its plan to exact increased profit transfers this year and next from the central bank through the higher valuation of its gold reserves.

The simple fact that Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing described the plan as "even more creative" than the accounting methods of other EMU-contender countries plays into the hands French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin.

Jospin, whose party supports EMU but wants a non-dogmatic interpretation of the Maastricht treaty and backs early entry for Italy and Spain, seized on the gold plan on Wednesday as proof that Bonn was resorting to a "fudge" in a country which had always espoused strictest adherence to the EMU treaty.
"Our German friends, who are so rigorous about the criteria, are looking to see if they can fudge things," Jospin told French RTL radio on Tuesday.

Jospin, whoses Socialists took a lead along with other left-wing parties over the centre-right ruling coalition in the first round election vote last Sunday, used Bonn's plan to support his case on interpretation of the EMU entry criteria.
The Socialist position, however, is not far from that of the current centre-right coalition, even if Jospin has made more capital out of the latest German manoeuvres.

Both positions use the room for manoeuvre available in the Maastricht treaty, which does not say public deficits have to be precisely 3.0 percent of gross domestic produce and leaves room for interpretation on debt control as well.

Economists in France and other EU states said on Wednesday that the Bundesbank's condemnation of the plan was remarkable for its strength. Economists said it was still not totally clear how the money would be used by Bonn in terms of Maastricht mathematics.

But it could end up being read as artful accounting by a country where this had long been deemed unacceptable and this could in turn make EMU qualification easier for EU countries with less robust EMU credentials, like Italy.
"If the government went against the Bundesbank -- and Issing is saying this is a wonderful accounting trick -- the door seems open to Italy," said Gwynne Hacche at HSBC James Capel.

"It reminds us once more that the Bundesbank is not willing to accept anything. If Germany used that (gold revaluation for EMU purposes), the possibility of excluding Italy would have been very limited," said JP Morgan economist David Naude.
It appears from a statement it issued on Wednesday that the German government wants to dedicate the extra funds to debt reduction rather than deficit reduction.
